title: Bamboo: the grass that behaves like a tree
text:
Walk through a bamboo grove on a still afternoon and you will hear it creak and click, as if the whole forest were whispering. Many people assume that bamboo is a tree, but it is actually a giant grass, a relative of the lawn grass in a garden and of the rice growing in the paddies. It is also one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth.

Some kinds of bamboo can grow up to ninety centimetres in a single day. That is nearly as tall as a three-year-old child, and you could almost watch it happen. The stems, called culms, shoot up from underground stems called rhizomes. Most of the growth happens in a short season, and the new shoot reaches its full height in only a few months. After that, the culm does not get any taller, but it slowly hardens over the next few years.

Bamboo is hollow, with solid "knuckles" called nodes along the stem. This design makes it both light and astonishingly strong. For its weight, bamboo is remarkably strong, and it is very hard to snap when pulled. This is why builders in Indonesia, India and China have used it for centuries as scaffolding, even for tall buildings.

Bamboo also has uses that are surprising. In West Java, craftspeople turn it into the angklung, an instrument that makes a clear note when shaken. In Bali and Sulawesi, families build houses, fences and water pipes from it. The young shoots, known as rebung, are a favourite ingredient in curries and soups. Paper, floor boards, toothbrushes and even clothing fibre are now made from the plant too.

Because it grows so quickly, bamboo is sometimes called a sustainable material. If you cut a mature culm, the plant does not die, since the rhizomes stay in the soil and push up new shoots. Bamboo roots also hold soil together on riverbanks and steep slopes, which helps to prevent landslides.

Yet bamboo is not a magic answer to everything. Cutting too much too fast can damage a grove, and the long distances that processed bamboo travels can add to pollution. As with any resource, the key is to use it with care.
